title: EDR
summary: Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) is a class of endpoint agent that continuously records process, file, registry, network and identity telemetry from a host, applies behavioural analytics and signature logic to that stream, and gives responders the ability to query, isolate and remediate the endpoint remotely. Unlike legacy antivirus, which largely evaluated files at rest or on execution, EDR treats sequence and context as the primary signal: a signed administrative utility writing to a run key, a shell spawning from an office productivity process, or a credential store being read by an unexpected parent are all interesting regardless of whether any single artefact matches a known bad hash. Modern deployments typically combine a lightweight kernel or platform-level sensor, a local detection engine for offline resilience, and a cloud backend that correlates across the estate, performs retroactive hunting over retained telemetry, and drives automated response actions. Practitioners care about EDR because it is the main source of truth for host-level investigation: it answers who ran what, as whom, from where, and what happened next. Its weaknesses are equally important to understand. Coverage varies by operating system and kernel version, sensor tampering and driver-level evasion can blind the agent, high-volume environments generate alert fatigue that buries real intrusions, and telemetry retention windows constrain how far back an analyst can hunt after a slow-burn compromise is discovered. EDR also raises its own governance questions around data residency, privacy, and the handling of employee endpoint data, and its value collapses if the deployment is partial, the exclusions list is unmanaged, or nobody owns tuning. Effective programmes pair EDR with strong identity telemetry, network metadata and a documented triage workflow rather than treating the console as a self-contained security solution.
objectives: Explain what an EDR sensor collects at kernel and user level, and how that differs from classic antivirus file scanning.
Describe the detection pipeline from raw telemetry through behavioural analytics to an alert a tier-one analyst can action.
Design a triage workflow that uses process lineage, parent-child relationships and user context to separate true positives from benign administrative activity.
Identify the practical blind spots of EDR coverage, including unsupported platforms, kernel-level evasion and stale or over-broad exclusions.
Evaluate retention, data residency and privacy constraints when planning retroactive threat hunting on endpoint telemetry.
Write a containment procedure that uses EDR isolation and remote remediation without destroying volatile evidence needed for investigation.
